source.title: Cross-Trajectory Chimera Interventions Reveal Dissociable Roles of Weight Magnitude and Direction in Grokking

page_placements.theme: Functional similarity with representational variation across runs

record.tranche_reason: The study intervenes on norms and directions in independently trained grokking networks and measures delay and circuit-spectrum outcomes; these are conceptual tests of parts of the claim, using cross-trajectory interventions rather than the original training-curve analysis.
record.gate_note: The study tests two modular-arithmetic tasks at a 50% train/test split. Its own delay, circuit-spectrum, and cross-trajectory intervention results are recorded below. It does not report a training-set-size sweep or full train/test accuracy curves establishing the chance-to-near-perfect trajectory. Cited results from prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a chimera-intervention study that uses grokking as its setting. The only part bearing on a claim version is its own measurement of spectral circuit reorganization after the test-accuracy transition, 32 seeds per task (Section 7), which relates to V2's gradual-mechanism and cleanup account. The norm–delay, direction–identity and threshold results measure constructs no version names. The cross-seed spectral distinctness result cannot separate 'different algorithm' from 'same Fourier algorithm with different key frequencies', so it does not test V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that direction carries a transferable, donor-specific component of circuit identity, and that it transfers as a threshold switch between basins. The threshold's location is predicted by recipient norm, with high-norm recipients flipping early. Norm carries only a modest, distributed delay effect and no identity signal. Circuits keep reorganizing after grokking and no two seeds share a spectrum. They limit the scope to two cyclic-group tasks and one architecture.
record.recipe_differences: Uses cross-trajectory norm/direction recombination, continued training, and spectral circuit-identity measurements rather than the original grokking training-curve analysis; includes angle-matched random controls and optimizer-moment ablations.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are reported separately for modular addition and multiplication. The norm–threshold relation differs by recipient norm class; layer-restricted norm swaps lose the whole-vector delay effect. Transplanting Adam moments shifts thresholds modestly but does not remove the reported separation.

fits_no_version.finding: Implanting a donor's weight direction transfers donor-specific spectral circuit identity (40/40 recombinations); angle-matched random directions produce near-zero lean.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In grokking modular-arithmetic transformers, weight direction at a pre-grokking checkpoint carries portable, donor-specific circuit identity.

fits_no_version.finding: Transplanting the donor's norm shifts grokking delay only partway toward the donor (mean scores 0.28 and 0.41, about 30% of the way). The effect vanishes when restricted to single layer groups, and changing norm alone does not change identity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight norm has a modest, whole-vector-distributed influence on grokking delay and carries no circuit-identity information.

fits_no_version.finding: Final embedding spectra are distinct across all 32 seeds per task (mean pairwise similarity 0.18–0.20).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independent grokking runs end in distinct spectral fingerprints, which may reflect different key frequencies rather than different algorithms.

fits_no_version.finding: Identity transfer along a direction interpolation is threshold-like. The threshold separates perfectly by recipient-norm class across 20 pairs (high norm flips early) and survives Adam-moment transplantation. No row records this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Susceptibility of a grokking network's circuit identity to being overwritten depends on its weight norm.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says analysis scripts are released but gives no URL)
record.problems: One architecture and two related cyclic-group tasks; only 10 disjoint pairs per task for the main interventions. Circuit identity is an embedding-spectrum proxy rather than complete circuit equivalence. The norm–threshold result is a two-class separation based on pair selection, not a fitted continuous law. The text notes that layer-localization evidence uses three pairs per task and that the optimizer-state ablation's fine interpolation grid uses two representative pairs per task.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant reported result was omitted. The sparse-parity exploration is described as not reported as a cross-task replication because it used a different optimization regime.

untested.parts: No training-set-size sweep, no full train/test accuracy curves, and no delay-versus-data-size result; single 50% split.
Whether a continuous progress measure anticipates the accuracy jump; removal of memorizing components; no pre-jump trajectory of the spectral measure is reported.
Non-algorithmic data; initialization scale or weight norm as a lazy-to-rich switch.
Weight decay favouring an efficient circuit, critical dataset size, ungrokking; weight decay is fixed at 1.0.
Algorithm-level identity across seeds; only an embedding-spectrum proxy is reported, and it is confounded by key-frequency choice.
Optimizer or numerical artifacts as the cause of the delay. The Adam-moment ablation concerns identity transfer and thresholds, not whether the delay disappears.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the norm–delay rows to V1 and V5, but neither version's quantities (dataset size, weight-decay efficiency, ungrokking) are measured. The V6 'challenges' label is dropped: per-seed differences in Fourier key frequencies (known from Nanda et al.) would produce distinct spectra under the same algorithm. The threshold–norm results (Section 5, Figures 4 and 6) and the Adam-moment ablation (Table 1) are not rowed; they bear on no version, including V7. Single-author preprint; scripts are said to be released, but no URL is given.

versions.untested_parts: No training-set-size sweep; no direct result that smaller training sets require more optimization; no full train/test accuracy curve documenting training accuracy saturation, chance test accuracy, and a later jump.
Does not identify a Fourier algorithm forming gradually or show memorizing components being removed; does not test whether a progress measure predicts the behavioral jump.
Non-algorithmic data, initialization scale, weight norm as a lazy-to-rich switch, and other regimes.
LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
Does not test whether weight decay favors an efficient circuit over memorization, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
Circuit identity is measured by an embedding-spectrum proxy, not a complete test of algorithmic equivalence.
No controlled test of adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts.

relation.reason: The study's own Section 7 measurements bear on V2's gradual-mechanism component.

tranche.reason: Spectral tracking supplies a different measure bearing on gradual circuit consolidation in V2; the portability interventions otherwise address a separate question.

source_check.notes: Circuit identity is an embedding-spectrum proxy, not complete algorithmic equivalence. The 40 endpoint outcomes use two variants for each of 20 independent pairs.

statements.correction: Section 7: spectral similarity continues increasing after the accuracy transition. Section 3: one-layer transformer, p=59, AdamW, weight decay 1.0. Reproducibility Statement: full analysis scripts reported released; availability is not independently verified here.
statements.problem: The post-transition spectral-reorganization claim and training conditions are supported, but the assertion that this study reports no code conflicts with its Reproducibility Statement.

statements.correction: Section 4 and Figure 2: 40/40 sign-correct outcomes pooled across two variants and two tasks. Radial retains recipient direction and yields 10/10 A-like outcomes per task; reverse radial implants donor direction and yields 10/10 B-like outcomes per task. Angle-matched random-control means: −0.031 addition; −0.051 multiplication.
statements.problem: Section 4's 40/40 pools radial and reverse-radial variants; it is not solely the count for implanting donor B's direction into recipient A. The abstract uses the broader wording, but the detailed results clarify the denominator.
